title: Open question: Paul's justify—forensic only or also inward renewal?
source_text: XXXIV. Caeterum semper quaestio remanet quo sensu apud Paulum sumatur justificatio, ubi affirmat Deum justificare impium, & nos justificari gratis, per Dei gratiam, non ex operibus, sed fide. An, scilicet, ibi justificatio designet solum absolutionem quandam judicialem a reatu peccati, & quae sit ab hominis sanctificatione distincta, ut volunt Protestantes; an vero praeterea significet internam nostri renovationem, per Spiritus Sancti gratiam, in qua consistit nostra regeneratio & sanctificatio, ut volunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae. Ad quam quaestionem, Observamus primo, Ubi de ipsa re & doctrina convenit, neque Scripturae tribuitur sensus ab analogia fidei alienus, non multum laborandum & contendendum esse, circa diversam alicujus loci interpretationem, & variam hujus, aut illius vocis, in eo acceptionem, sed liberum cuique suum hac in re judicium linqui solere, & debere. Quemadmodum Protestantes, qui quoad rei summam inter se consentiunt, facile patiuntur quosdam ex suis, hanc ipsam justificandi vocem, certis in locis, aliter atque aliter accipere, ut Dan. 12. 3. Rom. 8. 30. 1. Cor. 6. 11. Tit. 3. 7. Apoc. 22. 11. Ubi quibusdam videtur sensus forensis retineri posse; alii vero aliter existimant; sicut supra pluribus a nobis expositum est.
pass_a_gloss: For the rest the question always remains in what sense justification is taken in Paul, where he affirms that God justifies the ungodly, and that we are justified freely, by the grace of God, not of works, but by faith. Whether, namely, justification there designates only a certain judicial absolution from the guilt of sin, and one distinct from man's sanctification, as the Protestants will; or whether besides it signifies our inward renewal through the grace of the Holy Spirit, in which our regeneration and sanctification consist, as the Doctors of the Roman Church will. To which question we observe first: Where there is agreement on the thing itself and the doctrine, and no sense alien to the analogy of faith is attributed to Scripture, one ought not to labor and contend much about a diverse interpretation of some place and a varied acceptation of this or that word in it, but each one's own judgment in this matter is wont to be, and ought to be, left free. Just as Protestants, who agree among themselves as to the sum of the matter, easily allow some of their own to take this very word of justifying in certain places otherwise and otherwise, as Dan. 12:3, Rom. 8:30, 1 Cor. 6:11, Tit. 3:7, Apoc. 22:11. Where to some the forensic sense seems able to be retained; others think otherwise; as has been set forth by us above at greater length.
pass_b_english: Still open: in Paul, is justify only forensic absolution (Protestants) or also Spirit-wrought renewal (Romans)?
Where doctrine agrees and analogy of faith holds, leave lexical liberty—Protestants already differ among themselves on Dan 12, Rom 8, etc.
